subject: Pathology
summary: Male reproductive pathology includes congenital, inflammatory and neoplastic disorders of the penis, testis, epididymis and prostate. Recognising patterns, staging disease and linking causes to clinical urgency guides management.

sections.p: Pathology of the male reproductive tract refers to any disease affecting the penis, testes, epididymis, vas deferens or prostate, diagnosed by history, exam and targeted investigations.
b: Diagnosis relies on correlating symptoms with physical findings and confirming with imaging, labs or histology.

sections.p: Neoplastic lesions use TNM staging; prostatitis is graded by severity (acute, chronic, chronic‑recurrent); testicular tumours are staged by tumor markers and imaging.
b: Staging predicts prognosis and guides treatment intensity.

sections.p: Most common causes differ by organ: penile cancer – HPV, chronic inflammation; epididymitis – sexually transmitted infections (Chlamydia, Gonorrhoea) or urinary pathogens; prostatitis – E. coli, TB; testicular cancer – germ‑cell neoplasia; infertility – varicocele, infection, hormonal imbalance.
b: Infections (STIs, urinary pathogens, TB, HIV) are frequent in low‑resource settings.
Non‑infectious: trauma, congenital anomalies, hormonal disorders, exposure to herbal toxins.

sections.p: Patients may report pain, swelling, discharge, urinary obstruction, palpable mass, infertility or systemic symptoms such as weight loss.
b: Acute epididymitis: unilateral scrotal pain, fever, dysuria.
Prostatitis: perineal pain, urinary frequency, painful ejaculation.
Testicular tumour: painless firm mass, sometimes hormonal signs.

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm the suspected pathology and assess extent.

t.b: What is the anatomy of the testis/epididymis and is there a mass or fluid? → Detects tumours, hydrocele, epididymal inflammation.
Do germ‑cell tumours exist? → Elevated levels support seminoma/non‑seminoma; normal does not exclude tumour.
Is infection present? → Guides antibiotic choice; if unavailable, treat empirically for common pathogens.
Is there prostate pathology (cancer, prostatitis)? → Elevated PSA suggests cancer or inflammation; consider age‑adjusted cut‑offs.
What is the local extent of a tumour or inflammatory mass? → Provides staging detail when ultrasound is inconclusive.

sections.p: Identify features that signal imminent harm or systemic spread.
b: Rapidly enlarging testicular mass → possible aggressive cancer.
Severe sepsis from epididymo‑orchitis.
Obstructive urinary retention from prostate cancer.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor response.
b: Acute bacterial epididymitis: 3rd‑generation cephalosporin or doxycycline (covers STIs); avoid fluoroquinolones in children.
Prostatitis: fluoroquinolone for Gram‑negative, add TMP‑SMX if TB suspected; avoid NSAIDs in renal failure.
Testicular cancer: radical inguinal orchiectomy followed by chemotherapy (cisplatin‑based) for non‑seminoma; avoid scrotal violation.

sections.p: Regular review ensures remission, detects recurrence and addresses fertility concerns.
b: Post‑orchiectomy: serial tumor markers and imaging every 3‑6 months for 2 years.
Chronic prostatitis: repeat PSA and symptom scores after 3 months of therapy.
Infertility work‑up: repeat semen analysis after treating varicocele or infection.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic male reproductive pathology.
b: Hydrocele vs. testicular tumour – both present as scrotal swelling.
Benign prostatic hyperplasia vs. prostate cancer – overlapping urinary symptoms.
Normal PSA does not exclude high‑grade prostate cancer in young men.
Negative ultrasound does not rule out early testicular carcinoma; consider MRI.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden testicular pain with nausea (possible torsion)
Blood in urine or severe urinary retention (possible obstructive cancer)

faq.q: Why is a scrotal ultrasound preferred first?
faq.a: It is quick, non‑invasive, and distinguishes solid tumours from fluid collections.
Yes, inflammation can raise PSA; repeat testing after treatment helps differentiate cancer.
When torsion is suspected or a testicular mass is palpable and imaging is inconclusive.

exam: Describe the diagnostic work‑up for a painless testicular mass.
List the most common infectious causes of epididymitis in a low‑resource setting.
Explain how PSA levels are interpreted in the context of prostatitis versus cancer.
